study_material.title: Data Visualization & Dashboards
study_material.introduction: A great analysis with a bad chart doesn't get acted on. This topic covers how to pick the right chart type, avoid the common ways charts mislead an audience, and what makes a dashboard genuinely useful rather than just decorative.
learning_objectives: Match the right chart type to the data relationship being shown
Identify at least 3 common ways charts mislead readers
Explain the difference between an operational and an executive dashboard
Describe pre-attentive attributes (color, size, position) and why they matter
Critique a chart for unnecessary chart junk / clutter

concepts.heading: 1. Matching Chart Type to Data Relationship
concepts.body: Comparison across categories -> bar chart. Trend over time -> line chart. Part-to-whole -> stacked bar or (sparingly) pie chart, only with few categories. Relationship between two numeric variables -> scatter plot. Distribution of a single variable -> histogram. Geographic pattern -> map. Choosing the wrong chart type for the relationship is the single most common visualization mistake.

concepts.heading: 2. How Charts Mislead
concepts.body: Truncated y-axis (not starting at zero) exaggerates small differences into what looks like a huge change. Dual y-axes with different scales can make unrelated trends look correlated. 3D charts distort the true size of segments. Cherry-picked time windows can make a flat or declining trend look like consistent growth. A trustworthy chart makes the honest comparison obvious at a glance.

concepts.heading: 3. Pre-attentive Attributes
concepts.body: Color, size, position and shape are processed by the brain before conscious attention - a red bar among gray ones, or one bar taller than the rest, is noticed instantly. Good visualization design uses this deliberately: highlight the one number that matters with color, and mute everything else, rather than making everything equally colorful (which highlights nothing).

concepts.heading: 4. Dashboards: Operational vs. Executive
concepts.body: Operational dashboards are used moment-to-moment by frontline teams to act immediately (e.g. a call-center queue monitor) - dense, real-time, detailed. Executive dashboards summarize high-level trends for strategic decisions (e.g. monthly KPI summary for leadership) - a handful of the most important numbers, updated less frequently, with drill-down available but not required. Designing one dashboard to serve both audiences usually satisfies neither.

formulas: Data-ink ratio (Tufte): ink used to display actual data / total ink used in the chart - higher is better, less clutter
Rule of thumb: if a chart needs a long caption to explain what it's showing, the chart itself needs to be redesigned
shortcut_methods: If asked to critique a chart, check the y-axis first - a non-zero baseline is the most common way to exaggerate a trend
For 'which chart type should I use', map the question to one of 5 buckets: comparison, trend, part-to-whole, relationship, distribution
When designing for executives, force yourself to cut to the 3-5 numbers that actually drive a decision - resist the urge to show everything
common_mistakes: Defaulting to pie charts for many categories - beyond 4-5 slices they become unreadable; a bar chart is almost always clearer
Adding unnecessary 3D effects, gradients or excessive gridlines ('chart junk') that add no information
Building one dashboard meant to serve both daily operational decisions and monthly executive summaries
study_material.summary: Good data visualization is chart-type selection matched to the relationship in the data, honest axes and scales, deliberate use of color/size to draw the eye to what matters, and a dashboard designed for one specific audience and decision, not everyone at once.
quick_revision_notes: Comparison=bar, Trend=line, Part-to-whole=stacked bar/pie, Relationship=scatter, Distribution=histogram
Truncated y-axis is the most common way charts mislead
Pre-attentive attributes (color, size) should highlight the one number that matters
Operational dashboards = real-time/detailed; Executive dashboards = few numbers, high-level

practice_questions.question: You want to show how monthly revenue has changed over the past 2 years. Which chart type fits best?
practice_questions.explanation: Line charts are the standard choice for showing a trend over a continuous time period.

practice_questions.question: A bar chart's y-axis starts at 90 instead of 0, making a change from 92 to 95 look like a massive jump. This is an example of:
options: A truncated axis exaggerating the apparent difference
practice_questions.correct_answer: A truncated axis exaggerating the apparent difference
practice_questions.explanation: Not starting the y-axis at zero for a bar chart visually exaggerates small differences, one of the most common ways charts mislead.

practice_questions.question: To show the relationship between advertising spend and sales across 50 products, which chart is most appropriate?
practice_questions.explanation: Scatter plots are designed to reveal the relationship between two numeric variables across many data points.

practice_questions.question: A call center wants a screen showing live queue length and wait times that agents check constantly during their shift. This is best described as:
practice_questions.explanation: Real-time, detailed, action-oriented views used moment-to-moment by frontline staff are operational dashboards, distinct from high-level executive summaries.

practice_questions.question: A leadership dashboard shows 40 metrics on one screen, all in different bright colors, updated in real time. What is the strongest critique?
options: Too many equally-emphasized metrics and colors make it hard to identify what actually matters - it should be reduced to a handful of key numbers with deliberate use of color
The dashboard needs more colors to be readable
Real-time updates are inappropriate for any dashboard
Executive dashboards should never use color
practice_questions.correct_answer: Too many equally-emphasized metrics and colors make it hard to identify what actually matters - it should be reduced to a handful of key numbers with deliberate use of color
practice_questions.explanation: When everything is colorful and emphasized equally, nothing stands out - good dashboard design deliberately limits scope and uses pre-attentive attributes (like color) sparingly to highlight what matters most, especially for an executive audience.
